key_insight: Passively rotating, flush-mounted discs can slightly reduce turbulent boundary-layer skin friction, but the benefit is small and only emerges after accounting for geometry-induced drag penalties and local flow changes.
engineering_relevance: The study informs low-power surface-texturing strategies for drag management in wall-bounded turbulence, especially where passive motion can be induced by the flow itself.
method: Wind-tunnel experiments on turbulent boundary layers with $Re_\tau=880$–1460 over 32 staggered rotating discs
Direct force measurements to separate total drag, disc-motion effects, and stationary-disc baseline
Particle image velocimetry plus the extended Elnahhas-Johnson skin-friction identity to diagnose mean-flow and slip contributions
evidence_signal: Experiments showed the full disc housing/cover system increased drag relative to a flat plate, while isolating disc motion revealed a 3% drag reduction versus stationary discs, with the direct slip effect found to be negligible.
watch_item: The practical benefit is constrained by added drag from cavities and cover plates, so geometry details and gap-flow interactions must be controlled carefully before any implementation.
paper_title: Turbulent boundary layers altered by passively rotating discs
